_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Mishna. Nor with an undomesticated animal: a gazelle or a hart.
rashi:a1.2: Nor with a slaughtered animal: even a slaughtered lamb.
rashi:a1.3: A tereifa: whose legs were cut off from the knee joint and above.
rashi:a1.4: A hybrid: a billy goat that mated with a ewe.
rashi:a1.5: A koy: it is uncertain whether it is an undomesticated animal or a domesticated animal.
rashi:a1.6: Because it is a lamb: since both a ewe and a goat are called seh [a lamb].
rashi:a1.7: If one gave it to a priest: the firstborn donkey.
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. There: with regard to the Paschal offering.
rashi:a2.2: All of these names: those in our mishna. The Paschal offering does not come from a calf or from an undomesticated animal, as it is written: “From the sheep or from the goats” (Exodus 12:5); nor from a slaughtered animal, since we require slaughter for the sake of the Paschal offering; and not from a hybrid either, since hybrids are not offered on the altar, as is taught below: “A bull or a sheep” excludes a hybrid.
rashi:a5.1: A ben pekua: one found alive inside a slaughtered animal. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 74a).
rashi:a6.1: In a pot [bedikula]: a cauldron. That is, it is like a slaughtered animal, and one does not redeem with a slaughtered animal.
rashi:a6.2: Or perhaps etc.: and all of these with which, as the mishna says, one may not redeem, we are speaking of where they are not equal in value [to the donkey]; for if they are equal in value, even [redeeming] with boiled vegetables is permitted.
rashi:a8.1: A ben pekua is unfit for the Paschal offering, since it is not offered on the altar, as is taught in the second chapter of Shechitat Ḥullin (38b): “When it is born” excludes one born by caesarean section.
rashi:a9.1: What purpose does “lamb” serve: and it is reasonable that it serves to exclude a ben pekua, which is like a slaughtered animal and is not a lamb; while “you shall redeem” includes a blemished one, a female and a two-year-old, since they are lambs.
rashi:a10.1: With a hybrid: which is two species, we redeem, as is taught in the mishna: Rabbi Eliezer permits with a hybrid. [Rashi writes the abbreviation ר״א, which can be read either Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Elazar.]
rashi:a12.1: A cow that gave birth to a goat of sorts, one may not redeem: since it is a calf.
rashi:a12.2: With a hybrid we redeem: and all the more so with one that resembles another species, and it would not need to teach it.
rashi:a13.1: It teaches us the halakha itself: and it does not come for the inference.
rashi:a14.1: Is it a hybrid?: said in astonishment. It is one that merely resembles [another species]!
rashi:a15.1: To what: is it stated that the Rabbis rendered one that resembles another species like a hybrid?
rashi:a15.2: If to sacrificial animals: that it is not offered on the altar, why do I need to make the animal that resembles another species depend on a hybrid? Just as it is obvious to us with regard to a hybrid, it is obvious to us with regard to one that resembles another species.
rashi:a16.1: If to a firstborn: to teach us that, like a hybrid, it is not consecrated as a firstborn; that is obvious, since “But the firstborn of an ox” is written, and it is excluded explicitly.
rashi:a17.1: If to exclude it from the tithe: that just as hybrids are not tithed, so too one that resembles another species is not.
rashi:a17.2: That is obvious; both derive from one verse, “under,” “under.” Here it is written: “Under the rod” (Leviticus 27:32), and with regard to sacrificial animals it is written: “Under its mother” (Leviticus 22:27). Just as there a hybrid and one that resembles another species are not [offered], as we excluded them above, so too with the tithe, a hybrid and one that resembles another species are not [tithed].
rashi:a17.3: For a firstborn donkey: that we do not redeem a firstborn donkey with it, as with a hybrid.
rashi:a18.2: “Passing,” “passing”: here it is written: “Whatever passes under the rod” (Leviticus 27:32), and with regard to the firstborn it is written: “You shall cause to pass to the Lord every one that opens the womb” (Exodus 13:12). Just as with a firstborn it is obligated, as we said, if it has some characteristics [of its mother], so too it should be obligated in the tithe.
rashi:a19.1: It teaches us: that the halakha of a hybrid applies to it, since “under,” “under” is derived from sacrificial animals. Just as it is not offered on the altar, as is said at the beginning of our chapter (Bekhorot 3b) that it is a permanent blemish and may be slaughtered on account of it, so too it is not consecrated as tithe.
rashi:a20.1: Disqualified consecrated animals: that were redeemed and go out to non-sacred status.
rashi:a21.1: Since he says: that a firstborn donkey is permitted for benefit before its redemption, the firstborn donkey is non-sacred, and he can redeem it with this [disqualified consecrated animal], since one cannot say that a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition.
rashi:a22.1: A prohibition does not take effect: the prohibition of the firstborn donkey does not take effect on the prohibition [already on the lamb], since an animal of disqualified consecrated animals retains sanctity even after its redemption, as they are prohibited in shearing and in labor.
rashi:a23.1: Since it does not seize its redemption: the lamb given in its stead has no sanctity.
rashi:a24.1: A gazelle and a hart: is written with regard to disqualified consecrated animals, as it is written: “Notwithstanding, you may slaughter and eat meat after all the desire of your soul” (Deuteronomy 12:15), and it is speaking of disqualified consecrated animals.
tosafot:a1.1: Rabbi Eliezer permits with a hybrid: we read “Rabbi Elazar,” and we do not read “Rabbi Eliezer.” And so it is proven in the chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 78a), where it says that according to Rabbi Elazar, who permits with a hybrid because it is a lamb, [the verse] serves only to exclude a hybrid; for what halakha? And it answers: for a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one, whose conception was from a non-kosher one. And [that is] not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua, since according to Rabbi Yehoshua that is derived from “a lamb of the sheep and a lamb of the goats,” and all the more so not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who permits [such an animal] earlier in our chapter. Evidently Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with Rabbi Elazar, and it is Rabbi Eliezer who disputes with Rabbi Yehoshua.
tosafot:a19.1: It teaches us that “under,” “under” is derived from peace offerings [Tosafot’s heading reads “peace offerings” where the Gemara has “sacrificial animals”]: and if you say: why do I need, with regard to a firstborn, “until it is an ox and its firstborn is an ox”? Let us derive “passing,” “passing” from the tithe! One can say: because “but” [akh] is written to obligate [an offspring with] some characteristics resembling its mother, therefore it is necessary to exclude one that resembles another species in this verse, so that we learn from it what “but” refers to. However, according to that tanna who excluded one that resembles another species above from a firstborn donkey twice, and so revealed it to us with regard to monetary sanctity, and the same applies to inherent sanctity, by this reasoning he could not have derived “some characteristics” from “but”; and perhaps he derives it from another verse.
tosafot:a24.1: Just as one may not redeem with a gazelle and a hart etc.: there is another exposition of “a gazelle and a hart” in the second chapter (below, Bekhorot 15a), which exempts them [disqualified consecrated animals] from the priestly gifts; and were it not for an exclusion in the verse, its fat would be permitted, and it would exempt them from [the prohibition of slaughtering] it and its offspring [on the same day]. And if you say: how do we make all these expositions, when in the chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (below, Bekhorot 33a) it says that “a gazelle and a hart” is written three times, and each one is brought for its own matter, and we do not expound these expositions from them at all?
gershom:a1.1: Nor with a tereifa: for example, one whose legs were cut off from the knee joint and above.
gershom:a2.1: Nor with a hybrid: with a lamb that comes from a goat and a ewe.
gershom:a3.1: Nor with a koy: which comes from a billy goat and a female gazelle.
gershom:a4.1: And Rabbi Elazar permits with a hybrid because it is a lamb: since its father and mother are both a species of domesticated animal. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads Rabbi Elazar where the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer.]
gershom:a5.1: If one gave it to a priest: the firstborn donkey.
gershom:a6.1: The priest may not keep it: [meaning] he should not break its neck until the priest designates a lamb in its stead, and it is his, because of the decree of the verse: “And if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck.”
gershom:a7.1: It is stated here “lamb”: “you shall redeem with a lamb”; and it is stated there, with regard to the Paschal offering, “a lamb… unblemished, a male, in its first year.”
gershom:a8.1: Just as there it excludes all of these names: because the Paschal offering is a sacrificial animal, and we say with regard to sacrificial animals: “A bull or a sheep” excludes a hybrid, “or a goat” excludes one that resembles another species, “when it is born” excludes one born by caesarean section.
gershom:a9.1: So too here: in this “you shall redeem with a lamb,” it excludes all of these names.
gershom:a10.1: A ben pekua: a live lamb that is found in the belly of a slaughtered animal.
gershom:a11.1: It is like meat in a pot: and it is like a slaughtered animal, and one does not redeem with it.
gershom:a12.1: For you derive “lamb,” “lamb” from the Paschal offering, and with regard to the Paschal offering we say: excluding one born by caesarean section, which is a ben pekua; and therefore one does not redeem [with it]. If so, just as there it must be a male etc.
gershom:a13.1: With one that resembles another species: that is, its father is a ram and its mother a ewe, but it resembles another species.
gershom:a14.1: With one that resembles another species, is it necessary?: since its father and mother are of one species.
gershom:a15.1: This: a cow that gave birth to a goat of sorts, one may not redeem, since we say it is a calf. But a ewe that gave birth, from a ram, to a goat of sorts, one may redeem with it. And learn from this that he holds that one may redeem with one that resembles another species. [An editor’s note in the printed text suggests a different reading here.]
gershom:a16.1: Rabbi Elazar would say to you: does the baraita teach “a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts”? It does not teach that explicitly; one only infers it. According to Rabbi Elazar, even though one can infer this, it did not need to teach us that, since if one redeems with a hybrid, all the more so with one that resembles another species. Rather, the baraita itself comes to teach us that one may not redeem with [the offspring of] a cow that gave birth to a goat of sorts.
gershom:a17.1: Do not say: that it is a full-fledged goat and one may redeem with it; rather, follow its mother, and it is a calf. And it is not dealing with one that resembles another species, but with this case itself.
gershom:a18.1: What is a hybrid? A ewe etc. It is explained thus: what is similar to a hybrid, which, though it is not a hybrid, the Rabbis rendered like a hybrid with regard to its prohibition? That is a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts; this is not a hybrid but one that resembles another species, and even so it is prohibited like a hybrid.
gershom:a19.1: And to what [halakha] does he say that it is prohibited like a hybrid? If to sacrificial animals, to offerings, what does Rabba bar Shmuel’s teaching tell us? That did not need to be taught to us, since from the verse that excludes a hybrid from sacrificial animals, from there one that resembles another species is also excluded from sacrificial animals, as it is taught: “A bull or a sheep” etc.
gershom:a20.1: And if it is to exclude one that resembles another species from firstborn status, that too is derived from a verse, as it is written: “But the firstborn of an ox”: only if it is an ox and its firstborn is an ox, which excludes one that resembles another species.
gershom:a21.1: And if to exclude it from animal tithe, “under,” “under” is derived from sacrificial animals: it is written with regard to tithe, “whatever passes under the rod,” and it is written with regard to sacrificial animals, “under its mother”; just as there it excludes one that resembles another species, so too with tithe. Rather, is it not necessary for a firstborn donkey, to teach us, in what Rabba bar Shmuel teaches, that one may not redeem with one that resembles another species? Then resolve [the dilemma] from here.
gershom:a22.1: No, actually: do not resolve it from here; it was necessary to exclude it from the tithe, in a case where it has some characteristics resembling its mother.
gershom:a23.1: Lest you say: “passing,” “passing” is derived from a firstborn. It is written with regard to tithe, “whatever passes under the rod,” and it is written with regard to a firstborn, “you shall cause to pass every one that opens the womb.” Just as with regard to a firstborn we say that when it has some characteristics resembling its mother it is obligated in firstborn status, so too with tithe let us say that when it has some characteristics it is obligated in the tithe.
gershom:a24.1: It teaches us: in what Rabba bar Shmuel teaches, that it is not [obligated], since “under,” “under” is derived from sacrificial animals.
gershom:a25.1: And we still do not know whether one may redeem [with one that resembles another species] or may not redeem.
gershom:a26.1: Disqualified consecrated animals: for example, blemished ones that were redeemed. Since he says that a firstborn donkey is permitted for benefit before its redemption, it is non-sacred, as it is permitted for benefit like non-sacred property. And one may redeem with an animal of disqualified consecrated animals, since, as it is permitted for benefit, there is no prohibition taking effect on a prohibition here; for disqualified consecrated animals carry a prohibition of shearing and of labor, as is said in the chapter below: “You may slaughter,” and not shear; “meat,” and not milk.
gershom:a27.1: Rather, when should you raise the dilemma? According to Rabbi Yehuda etc.: the prohibition of a firstborn donkey, which is prohibited for benefit, does not take effect on the prohibition of disqualified consecrated animals, which are prohibited in shearing and in labor; therefore one may not redeem.
gershom:a28.1: Or perhaps: since the sanctity of a firstborn donkey is not strong enough to seize its redemption so that it would be prohibited for benefit, and that which the Merciful One required redeeming it is merely an abrogation of the prohibition, so that the firstborn donkey becomes permitted for benefit, and not so that its sanctity takes effect on its redemption; so too its prohibition does not take effect at all on the prohibition of disqualified consecrated animals, and there is no prohibition taking effect on a prohibition here, and one may redeem with an animal of disqualified consecrated animals.
gershom:a29.1: Is that which is written with regard to them insignificant: with regard to disqualified consecrated animals: “You shall eat it within your gates, the impure and the pure alike, like the gazelle and like the hart”; and this “impure” is a blemished one. Just as one may not redeem with a gazelle and a hart, as we learned: one may not redeem with an undomesticated animal.
gershom:a30.1: Now that you have arrived at this: even according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits benefit, even so one may not redeem, since “a gazelle and a hart” is written with regard to them.
rashi:b1.1: According to Rabbi Shimon as well: even though he permits benefit from a firstborn donkey, one does not redeem it with disqualified consecrated animals, since “a gazelle and a hart” is written with regard to them.
rashi:b2.1: With a Sabbatical animal: an animal that was purchased with produce of the Sabbatical Year.
rashi:b3.1: A definite one, you should not raise the dilemma: about a definite firstborn donkey you should not ask, since he must give its redemption to the priest, he may not redeem it [with such an animal], as the Merciful One said “for consumption,” and not for commerce; and it turns out that he acquires a donkey, which is not fit to eat, with Sabbatical produce.
rashi:b3.2: Uncertain: for example, where its mother gave birth to a male and a female, where it says in the mishna that he designates a lamb and it is his own.
rashi:b4.1: And according to Rabbi Shimon you should not raise the dilemma: since according to him one need not designate a lamb to abrogate its prohibition when he does not give it to the priest, as Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from a firstborn donkey.
rashi:b6.1: The definite one: a definite firstborn donkey, because he must give it to the priest, and it is commerce.
rashi:b7.1: In the gifts: the foreleg, the jaw and the maw.
rashi:b8.1: For burning: and if it were obligated as a firstborn, its sacrificial portions would go up to the Most High [i.e., be burned on the altar].
rashi:b9.1: Impure ḥalla has no remedy except burning, since one who eats impure teruma is liable to death.
rashi:b10.1: And why: is dough of Sabbatical produce obligated in ḥalla in the Sabbatical Year?
rashi:b11.1: “Throughout your generations”: is written with regard to ḥalla, implying even in the Sabbatical Year; and it is written: “Of the first of your dough” etc. (Numbers 15).
rashi:b12.1: This is also taught: that the reason is because “throughout your generations” is written with regard to it.
rashi:b13.1: And let him derive from it: that [the verse] does not say “for consumption” and not for burning, and a Sabbatical animal would be obligated in firstborn status.
rashi:b13.2: There: with regard to ḥalla, the primary purpose of its separation is for eating, since it is burned only if it became impure.
rashi:b14.1: To keep it: even for one moment.
rashi:b15.1: Are suspect: that they work with them without redemption.
rashi:b15.2: Obvious: since we certainly learn it from here.
rashi:b15.3: Lest you say this applies: that he should not give it to him [only] where we have a presumption that he happens to be suspect, that we have seen him suspected in the matter. Another version: that it happens, that we saw him chance to work with a firstborn donkey before its redemption.
rashi:b15.4: That he grants himself permission in it: since he reasons: since the lamb I would designate in its stead would be mine, why do I need to redeem it?
rashi:b16.1: Mishna. Like the five sela of the redemption of a son: as is said in the chapter Yesh Bekhor LaNaḥala (below, Bekhorot 51a), that he bears responsibility for it.
rashi:b16.2: Like the redemption of second tithe: that if it was lost, he does not bear responsibility for it, according to the Rabbis.
rashi:b17.1: The firstborn donkey died: after he designated its redemption and had not yet given it to the priest.
rashi:b17.2: Rabbi Eliezer says: It must be buried: since he bears responsibility for the lamb, it is as though he had not designated it, and the Israelite is permitted to benefit from the lamb as one who had not designated it.
rashi:b17.3: It does not need to be buried: since from the moment he designated the lamb it stands in the priest’s possession, and the firstborn donkey is redeemed.
rashi:b18.1: Gemara. Bears responsibility for it: if he designated its redemption and it was lost.
rashi:b19.1: Is permitted for benefit: before its redemption.
rashi:b20.1: It must be buried like a firstborn person: not because it is prohibited for benefit, but because it is compared to a firstborn person, and an ordinary firstborn person is given to burial.
rashi:b21.1: Rabbi Eliezer concedes: although with a definite firstborn donkey he holds that as long as [its redemption] has not reached the priest’s hand it is not redeemed, he concedes with an uncertain one that he need not give the redemption to the priest, but designates etc. And since he requires designating a lamb to abrogate its prohibition, by inference he holds that a firstborn donkey is prohibited for benefit.
rashi:b22.1: I compared it with regard to redemption: [I compared] the firstborn of a non-kosher animal to a firstborn person, that he bears responsibility for its redemption, and not with regard to another matter, for benefit.
rashi:b23.1: Valuations at their time: that if at the time he said “My valuation is upon me” he was from one month to five years old, and he waited and did not give it until he was six, when he has a different valuation, as is written in the passage of valuations (Leviticus 27), even so he gives only according to the time at which he made the valuation.
rashi:b23.2: After thirty: as it is written: “And their redemption money, from a month old” etc. (Numbers 18:15–16).
rashi:b24.1: And redemption of a firstborn donkey is immediate?: said in astonishment.
rashi:b24.2: There are no valuations for less than thirty days: such a one is not valuated, as is written in the passage.
rashi:b24.3: And of naziriteship: an unspecified naziriteship is thirty days, as it is written: “He shall be [yihyeh] holy” (Numbers 6:5), and yihyeh in gematria is thirty.
rashi:b25.1: And one may add: since there is a valuation for every age at which he stands, as is written in the passage; and likewise a nazirite may vow a naziriteship of four or five years; and if he waited several years with the redemption of his son or the redemption of his firstborn donkey, he can still redeem it, and he does not give more.
rashi:b26.1: To say that if he redeemed it, it is redeemed: that which was taught above, “redemption of a firstborn donkey is immediate,” means that if he redeemed it immediately it is [redeemed], but he does not fulfill the primary mitzva of redemption.
rashi:b26.2: By inference, his son: since you established it as after the fact, and it teaches that a son is after thirty, by inference if he redeemed him within thirty he is not redeemed.
rashi:b26.3: But wasn’t it stated: in the chapter Yesh Bekhor LaNaḥala (below, Bekhorot 49a).
rashi:b27.1: Everyone agrees, “from now”: where he said to him: Let this redemption take effect from now, he is not redeemed. Where they disagree is where he said: I am giving the money now, and the redemption will not take effect until after thirty days.
tosafot:b3.1: A definite one, you should not raise the dilemma: “for consumption, and not for commerce” implies that it is prohibited to purchase a non-kosher animal, such as a firstborn donkey, with Sabbatical produce. And this is puzzling, for even the Rabbis prohibit only soaking and laundering [with Sabbatical produce], in the first chapter of HaGozel (Bava Kamma 102a), because we require [a use] similar to “for consumption,” where its benefit and its consumption coincide; and an animal for labor is [a case] where its benefit and its consumption coincide.
tosafot:b10.1: Since if it became impure etc.: and even though he could separate [ḥalla] for this dough from another dough that is not of the Sabbatical Year, joining the two, nevertheless this one is not subject to ḥalla and he cannot separate from it itself; it is like [separating] from the obligated for the exempt.
tosafot:b13.1: Here the primary purpose is for burning: Rabbeinu Tam asked: let us derive from the omer, whose primary purpose is for burning. For it says in the chapter Kol Korbanot (Menaḥot 84a): the guards of the aftergrowth in the Sabbatical Year would take their wages from the collection of the Temple chamber; and it asks: how does one bring the omer from Sabbatical produce? The Merciful One said “for consumption,” and not for burning, and there is the handful that is offered on the altar! [And it answers:] There it is different, as the verse states: “Throughout your generations.” One can say: we do not derive a firstborn from the omer, as there are many refutations: what is notable about the omer is that it is a communal offering and overrides Shabbat and impurity. And furthermore, it is impossible to fulfill the omer in the Sabbatical Year except with Sabbatical produce, since we require fresh grain; but firstborn status and ḥalla can be fulfilled in the Sabbatical Year with other animals and other produce.
tosafot:b27.1: Wasn’t it stated with regard to that: Rava says: Everyone agrees that with “from now” he is not redeemed: this wording is not found below, in the chapter Yesh Bekhor (Bekhorot 49a; see there).
gershom:b1.1: With a Sabbatical animal: with a lamb that was purchased with produce of the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b2.1: A definite firstborn donkey, you should not raise the dilemma, since one may not redeem with a Sabbatical animal, as the Merciful One said “for consumption” (and the animal has [the status] of the produce), and not for commerce; and this is commerce, that he redeems the firstborn donkey with this lamb.
gershom:b3.1: When should you raise the dilemma? An uncertain one: whether he can redeem an uncertain firstborn donkey with it.
gershom:b4.1: And according to Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold [that anything is required for] an uncertain one, [as] at the beginning of our discussion: “and since it is for himself, why do I need to designate” etc. And we said [above]: our mishna is Rabbi Yehuda, as it teaches etc., and Rabbi Shimon permits; it was thought that Rabbi Shimon permits, since one need not designate at all, as it is uncertain.
gershom:b5.1: You should not raise the dilemma: since it is permitted to redeem, for this is not commerce, since even without redemption it would be permitted.
gershom:b6.1: When should you raise the dilemma? According to Rabbi Yehuda: who requires designating to abrogate its prohibition.
gershom:b7.1: What is the halakha? Since he designates a lamb and it is his own, we call it “for consumption,” since it is his own.
gershom:b8.1: Or perhaps, since as long as he has not abrogated the prohibition with this lamb, this firstborn donkey is not permitted to him for benefit, it is like commerce, for he acquires its benefit with this lamb, and it is prohibited.
gershom:b9.1: One may not redeem with it the definite one: a firstborn donkey, since that is commerce.
gershom:b10.1: But one may redeem with it the uncertain one: since it is not full commerce, as it is only uncertain.
gershom:b11.1: And Rav Ḥisda says: it is exempt from firstborn status, since the Merciful One said “for consumption,” and not for burning, and the sacrificial portions of a firstborn stand to be burned; and it is obligated in the gifts, the foreleg and the jaw, which stand to be eaten. At any rate, Rav Ḥisda’s teaching tells us that one may redeem the uncertain one with it.
gershom:b12.1: Before its ḥalla was separated, is liable to death: as it is written: “And they shall not bear sin for it” etc.
gershom:b13.1: And why is he liable to death? Since if the ḥalla became impure it stands to be burned, and the Merciful One said “for consumption,” and not for burning, one should not be liable for ḥalla, since it has a law of burning, just as you exempted it from firstborn status because the sacrificial portions stand to be burned.
gershom:b14.1: This is not difficult, why he is liable to death in the Sabbatical Year: because it is written with regard to ḥalla “throughout your generations,” as it is written: “You shall give to the Lord a gift throughout your generations”: its prohibition always applies, even in the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b15.1: And let him derive from it: from ḥalla to firstborn status, that it too should be obligated in firstborn status.
gershom:b16.1: It is not similar; there, it is for this reason that he is liable to death for it: because the primary purpose of ḥalla is to be eaten by the priest, and not to become impure and be burned.
gershom:b17.1: Here: with regard to a firstborn, the primary purpose of the sacrificial portions is for burning and not for eating; therefore it is exempt from firstborn status, as the Merciful One said “for consumption,” and not for burning.
gershom:b18.1: We learn it: in our mishna as well, this baraita that the Sages taught, because it [the mishna] is primary.
gershom:b19.1: Unless he redeemed it: unless the priest redeemed it in his presence.
gershom:b20.1: That is to say: since it says “unless he redeemed it in his presence,” learn from it that priests are suspect with regard to firstborn donkeys, that they will not redeem them.
gershom:b21.1: Obvious: since in the baraita we see explicitly that they are suspect; so what does Rav Naḥman teach us?
gershom:b22.1: Lest you say: were it not for Rav Naḥman, I would have said that this, that one should not give it to him unless he redeemed it in his presence, applies only where we have a presumption about that one, that he is not so learned and it happens that he does work with it before he redeems it.
gershom:b23.1: But in an ordinary case: where we have no such presumption, I would say he need not redeem it in his presence, since they are not suspect. It teaches us that all of them are suspect.
gershom:b24.1: Because they grant themselves permission in it, saying: what need is there for me to redeem it? When I redeem it, the lamb will be mine, and now it is mine; and he does not bother to redeem it. Therefore one should not give it to him unless he redeemed it in his presence.
gershom:b25.1: One who designates the redemption of a firstborn donkey and it died: before it came into the priest’s hand, the Israelite bears responsibility for it, to give him another redemption, like the five sela of a son, as we learned in the chapter Yesh Bekhor LaNaḥala: one who designates the redemption of his son and it was lost bears responsibility for it, as it is stated: “Yet you shall surely redeem.”
gershom:b26.1: And the Rabbis say: he does not bear responsibility for it, like the redemption of second tithe: just as with second tithe, if its redemption was lost he does not bear responsibility for it, since it is his, except that he must bring it up and eat it in Jerusalem when he has [the means] to bring it up, and if not he is exempt; so too with the redemption of a firstborn [donkey], he does not bear responsibility for it. Rabbi Yehoshua testified, and it is all in accordance with the Rabbis.
gershom:b27.1: The firstborn donkey died: before the lamb came into the priest’s hand.
gershom:b28.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: It must be buried: since it is prohibited for benefit, as at first.
gershom:b29.1: And it is permitted: the Israelite is permitted to benefit from the lamb.
gershom:b30.1: And the Rabbis say: It does not need to be buried: and its hide and carcass are permitted for benefit.
gershom:b31.1: And the lamb goes to the priest: since from the time he designated it, it stands in the priest’s possession.
gershom:b32.1: Abaye said to him: since he compares it to a firstborn person, let him compare it in every matter as well, and say: if so, just as with a firstborn person the benefit of his labor is permitted, so too with the firstborn of a non-kosher animal.
gershom:b33.1: And if you would say: indeed. But didn’t we learn: it died etc.? No, actually it is permitted for benefit as well; and what is meant by “it must be buried”? Not because it is prohibited for benefit, but since he compares it to a firstborn person, it must also be buried like a firstborn person.
gershom:b34.1: But if so, is it a firstborn person who requires burial? That is, if for this reason he said “it must be buried,” not that it is prohibited for benefit but that it requires burial, let him say “it must be buried like a person.” Rather, since he said “it must be buried,” learn from it that it is prohibited for benefit.
gershom:b35.1: And furthermore, it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer concedes that one designates a lamb for it, and it is his. Evidently, if he does not designate, it is prohibited for benefit, and all the more so a definite firstborn donkey. And since he did not compare it with regard to benefit, he should not compare it with regard to responsibility either.
gershom:b36.1: Rava says: actually, we compare it with regard to redemption, for responsibility, and not for benefit; and we learn this from the verse itself, as it is written: “Yet you shall surely redeem”: I compared it to a firstborn person with regard to redemption, and not with regard to another matter, for benefit.
gershom:b37.1: Valuations at their time: that if he valuated a minor and afterward the minor grew up, he need give only according to the time at which he valuated him. And the redemption of a son he is obligated to give only after thirty [days], since until thirty we are concerned that he may be a non-viable newborn.
gershom:b38.1: And a firstborn donkey immediately: one redeems it even within thirty [days]. And one raises a contradiction: there are no valuations [for less than thirty days], since one less than a month old has no valuation; and there is no naziriteship of less than thirty [days], as it is written: “He shall be [yihyeh] holy,” which in gematria is thirty; and the redemption of a son and the redemption of a firstborn donkey [do] not [apply] in less than thirty days.
gershom:b39.1: And one may add forever: since from thirty [days] and up one can valuate him forever, and there is an increase in valuation when he is older.
gershom:b40.1: And in naziriteship: that if he wants to add to thirty as much as he wishes, forever, it is permitted. And the redemption of a son and of a firstborn donkey: from thirty and up he can redeem them forever; and that is “and one may add to them.” But in their redemption there is no addition of value: as much as he would give when they are thirty days old, so he gives at any time he wishes to redeem them. Evidently one does not redeem a firstborn donkey in less than thirty days.
gershom:b41.1: Rav Naḥman said that Rav said: what is meant by “immediately” that it states? To say that if he redeemed it immediately, it is exempt after the fact. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “Rav Naḥman said that Rav said”; the daf reads “Rav Naḥman says.”]
gershom:b42.1: By inference: the Rabbis of the baraita that says “there are no valuations” hold that if he redeemed [his son] before [thirty days], he is not redeemed, even after the fact. But wasn’t it stated etc.? If so, what is the difference between them? And one cannot answer as you said, “to say that if he redeemed it, it is redeemed,” for all cases, as we answered. And as for what is difficult, “but wasn’t it stated: one who redeems” etc.: wasn’t it stated with regard to that: everyone agrees that with “from now,” that is, where he said within thirty [days], “This is his redemption, that he be redeemed from now,” before thirty, his son is not redeemed even after the fact, because when he says “from now” it is as if he wants the mitzva to be now as well, and it is not [its time] until thirty. Evidently the Rabbis hold that if he redeemed him, he is not redeemed.
